modules.title: Intro to Computers & AI
modules.concept: How computers work and what AI is

markdown: Have you ever wondered how your phone knows which video you want to watch next?
In AI Academy, you will find out how computers and artificial intelligence (AI) really work.
You do not need any experience. You just need to be curious.
## What you will learn
AI Academy has six modules. Each one builds on the last.
1. Computers and how they process information
2. AI history and common AI technologies
3. Problem-solving with Scratch and Python
4. Data, patterns, and prediction
5. Ethics, sustainability, and social good
6. A community AI project (capstone)
## Course goals
By the end, you will be able to:
- Explain how computers and AI systems work
- Build confidence through hands-on projects
- Practice critical thinking and problem-solving
- Judge AI's benefits, risks, and limits
- Design and present an AI idea for a real need in your community
## How we learn together
These six norms help everyone do their best work.
- **Be curious.** Questions are always welcome.
- **Try first.** Give it a shot before saying, "I can't."
- **Help without taking over.** Support your team and let everyone do their part.
- **Critique ideas, not people.** Be kind when you give feedback.
- **Use AI honestly.** Say when AI helped you, and protect personal information.
- **Make something you are proud of.** Then share it!
> **Remember:** Never type personal information, like your full name, address, or phone number, into an AI tool.

markdown: Look around you. How many computers can you spot?
You might see a laptop or a phone. There could also be computers hiding inside a microwave, a TV, or a car.
## So what is a computer?
A **computer** is an electronic device that processes data and performs tasks based on instructions.
The list of instructions is called a **program**.
> **Key idea:** A computer follows a program to process data. It does not think for itself. It follows its instructions one at a time, very fast.
## What can a computer do?
Computers help us learn, create, communicate, and solve problems.
Here are four things they do well:
- **Work fast.** A computer can do millions of math problems in a second.
- **Store information.** It can keep huge amounts of photos, music, and schoolwork.
- **Connect to networks.** It can reach the internet and other computers.
- **Help people communicate.** Think of messages, video calls, and email.
> **Did you know?** A computer does not see words or pictures the way you do. Inside, it stores everything as 0s and 1s. You will see how soon.
What really happens when you type a word and click Save?
Your information takes a quick trip through four kinds of parts.
## The four kinds of parts
| Part | What it does | Examples |
| **Input** | Brings information in | Keyboard, mouse, microphone, touch screen |
| **Processing** | Follows the program's instructions | CPU (processor) |
| **Memory and storage** | Holds data and programs | RAM, SSD or hard drive |
| **Output** | Shows or plays the result | Screen, speaker, printer |
The **CPU** is sometimes called the computer's "brain".
While it works, it trades information with memory and storage all the time.
## Memory vs. storage
These two sound alike, but they do different jobs.
- **RAM** (memory) is short-term. It holds what you are using right now, and it is cleared when the power goes off.
- An **SSD** or hard drive (storage) is long-term. It keeps your files even when the power is off.
> **Watch out:** RAM does not keep your work when the power goes off. Clicking Save copies your work to storage, so it is safe.
## Example: typing and saving your work
1. You press keys on the keyboard. **(input)**
2. The CPU follows the word processor's instructions. **(processing)**
3. Your words sit in RAM while you type. **(memory)**
4. The letters appear on the screen. **(output)**
5. You click Save, and the file is written to the SSD. **(storage)** It will still be there tomorrow.
## Everything is 0s and 1s
Inside, a computer turns all information into **binary**: long patterns of 0s and 1s.
Each 0 or 1 is called a **bit**.
Letters, colors, sounds, and videos are all stored as bits.
> **Key idea:** Input brings data in, the CPU processes it, memory and storage hold it, and output shows the result. A program tells the computer how to use the data.

markdown: What do you think the oldest computing machines looked like?
Long before screens and keyboards, some machines that did math were made of metal gears.
## The Difference Engine
In **1822**, an English inventor named **Charles Babbage** proposed a machine called the **Difference Engine**.
It was a **mechanical calculator**.
It used gears and number wheels, not electronic circuits, to work out tables of numbers.
> **Watch out:** The Difference Engine was not a general-purpose computer. It could do only one kind of job: calculating. A laptop can run many different programs.
Babbage never finished building it.
In 1991, a museum in London built a later design of his, the **Difference Engine No. 2**, from his plans.
> **Did you know?** The finished Difference Engine No. 2 weighs about 5 tons. That is about as heavy as a large elephant!
## Think of a coin sorter
A coin sorter can help you picture how the Difference Engine worked.
Both machines follow the same three steps:
1. **Input:** they take something in. A coin sorter takes a pile of mixed coins.
2. **Processing:** moving parts do the work, with no electronics.
3. **Output:** they give a result. A coin sorter gives stacks of sorted coins, and the Difference Engine gave a table of answers.
> **Key idea:** Input, processing, output. Early machines followed the same pattern as modern computers, just with gears instead of circuits.
The Difference Engine used gears you could watch turn.
Your phone uses tiny electronic circuits you cannot even see.
A lot has changed since 1822!
## Side by side
| | Difference Engine No. 2 | A modern laptop |
| **Parts** | Metal gears and number wheels | Electronic circuits on chips |
| **Size** | About 5 tons, with about 8,000 parts | About 1 to 2 kilograms |
| **Speed** | Only as fast as a person turns its handle | Billions of steps every second |
| **Tasks** | One job: calculating number tables | Many programs: games, maps, video calls, AI apps |
| **Input** | Turning number wheels by hand | Keyboard, touch pad, microphone, camera |
> **Key idea:** Both machines automate calculation with physical parts. The big difference is that a modern computer can run many different programs.
## How computers changed
- **Size:** some early electronic computers filled a whole room. Today, a much more powerful computer fits in your pocket.
- **Speed:** modern computers are far faster and more powerful.
- **Tasks:** early computers did basic calculations. Modern computers do much more.
- **Input:** many early computers needed punch cards or switches. Today we type, tap, click, and talk.
## Computers hiding in plain sight
Phones, tablets, and laptops are computers.
So are many other things:
- Game consoles and smart TVs
- Car dashboards
- Microwaves and digital watches
> **Try it:** Look around the room. Find one thing with a computer inside that is not a phone, tablet, or desktop.

markdown: You have probably used AI today without noticing.
Maybe an app suggested a song, or your phone unlocked when it saw your face.
So what makes something AI?
> **Think about it:** Before you read on, how do you think AI works? Name one place you have seen it.
## A working definition
**Artificial intelligence (AI)** is a big field of computer science.
AI systems are computer systems that do tasks like **recognizing patterns**, **understanding language**, or **making predictions**.
These are tasks that usually need human thinking.
## How does AI learn?
Many AI systems today learn from **examples**.
This is called **machine learning**.
Say you want a computer to spot cats in photos.
People show it thousands of photos labeled "cat" or "not cat".
The computer finds patterns in those examples, then uses the patterns to guess about a new photo it has never seen.
> **Key idea:** In machine learning, a computer finds patterns in training examples and uses them on new inputs.
> **Watch out:** Not every AI system uses machine learning. Some AI follows rules that people wrote by hand. But many AI tools you use every day do learn from examples.
## Automatic does not mean AI
A machine that does something by itself is not always AI.
Ask: does it recognize patterns, understand language, or make predictions?
| Example | AI or not? | Why |
| Automatic door | Not AI | A sensor notices motion and the door opens. It follows the same rule every time. |
| Kitchen timer | Not AI | It counts down and beeps. It learns nothing and predicts nothing. |
| Translation app | AI | It understands language and rewrites it in another language. |
| Face unlock on a phone | AI | It recognizes the patterns of your face. |
| Robot vacuum | Depends | A basic one just bumps and turns. Some newer ones use AI to recognize objects and map rooms. |
Next, you will sort more examples yourself.

activities.title: What can AI do, and where can it go wrong?

markdown: AI can write a poem in seconds and find one face in thousands of photos.
But AI can also be wrong while sounding completely sure.
Knowing both sides helps you use AI wisely.
## What AI can and cannot do well
| AI is good at... | But AI can... |
| **Finding patterns**, like spotting a cat in a photo | **Miss context** that a person would notice |
| **Making predictions**, like guessing which movie you will like next | **Be unfair (biased)** if its examples were unfair |
| **Creating text or images**, like drafting a message from your prompt | **State wrong facts** in a confident voice |
| **Understanding speech and language**, like a voice assistant answering a question | **Give unreliable answers** that change when you ask again |
> **Watch out:** More data does not automatically make an AI better. If the examples are wrong or unfair, more of them will not fix the problem.
## Think like an AI designer
> **Try it:** Pick a task: recommending a movie, identifying a photo, or drafting a message. Answer these three questions in your head or on paper.
> 1. What information would the AI need?
> 2. What could it produce?
> 3. Where could it make a mistake?
Here is one example.
A movie app needs to know what you watched before, and it uses that to suggest new movies.
It could be wrong if your little brother used your account!
## Before you trust an AI answer
Check it with a trusted source, like a textbook, a teacher, or a reliable website.
> **Key idea:** AI is a useful tool, but it can make mistakes. Always check before you trust.

content.prompt: A chatbot tells you a fact for your history project. What is the best next step?

choices.label: Use it right away, because AI does not make mistakes
Ask the chatbot if it is sure, and trust whatever it says
Change a few words so it looks like your own

content.explanation: AI can state wrong facts confidently. Checking a trusted source is how you know the fact is right.

markdown: When people hear "AI", many think of chatbots.
But AI is also inside lots of apps you already use.
## Five common AI technologies
| Technology | What it does | Example |
| **Smart assistants** | Understand your voice and answer questions | Siri, Alexa |
| **Recommendation systems** | Suggest videos, songs, or products based on patterns in what you and others liked | Video and music apps |
| **Chatbots** | Write answers to your messages using patterns learned from lots of text | AI chat apps |
| **Facial recognition** | Find and match faces in photos | Unlocking a phone with your face |
| **Navigation apps** | Predict traffic and suggest the fastest route | Map apps on a phone or in a car |
> **Did you know?** Siri first came out on the iPhone in 2011. That means smart assistants have been in people's pockets for about 15 years.
## Your turn: AI scavenger hunt
> **Try it:** Pick one of the five technologies. Look it up with a trusted source and find:
> 1. How it works, in your own words
> 2. One surprising fact
> 3. Where you found the information
> **Think about it:** Which AI apps do you use in your everyday life? What does the AI do in each one?

markdown: Time to be a tech detective!
You will pick a real AI app, test it with three kinds of prompts, and report what you find.
**Goal:** research and test an AI application.
> **Remember:** Never type personal information into an AI tool. That means no full name, address, phone number, school name, passwords, or photos of yourself or friends.
## Steps
1. **Choose an app.** Pick one AI app your teacher or a parent says is OK. Check the app's age rules, because many chatbots are only for ages 13 and up.
2. **Describe it.** Write down its purpose and three key features.
3. **Test it.** Try one prompt from each of the three groups below.
4. **Summarize.** Write a short summary of each response.
5. **Judge it.** Name one strength and one limitation of the app.
6. **Share it.** Get ready to explain your app to a friend in one minute.
## Pick your prompts
### 1. Fact-checking
These test whether the AI gives accurate information.
Pick one:
- What are the three laws of motion?
- What is the Pythagorean Theorem used for?
- When did World War II end and who were the major powers involved?
> **Try it:** Check the AI's answer against your textbook or another trusted source. Was it right?
### 2. Creative writing
These test how well the AI writes creative or clear text.
Pick one:
- Can you write a short story about a robot that learns to feel emotions?
- Can you help me write a poem about climate change in the style of Dr. Seuss?
- Rewrite this paragraph to sound more professional. (Paste a paragraph you wrote about a school topic, with nothing personal in it.)
### 3. Capabilities and limits
These help you find out what the AI can and cannot do.
Pick one:
- Can you explain how you were trained?
- Do you have access to real-time news?
- Can you tell me who won the Super Bowl last weekend?
> **Think about it:** If the AI answers the Super Bowl question, how could you tell whether its answer is up to date?
## What to turn in
When you are done, fill in the worksheet in this lesson.
It asks for:
- The app and its purpose
- Three key features
- Your three prompts, with a short summary of each answer
- One strength and one limitation
- One question you still have
- What you would say to explain the app in one minute
